analysis.one_liner: Makes offshore oil companies pay all oil spill cleanup costs instead of capping their liability at $75 million.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the $75 million oil spill liability cap never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster, this bill would have removed the $75 million cap on what a company must pay when its offshore rig spills oil, making it responsible for every cleanup and damage dollar [S2, S3]. It would even have applied retroactively to spills from April 15, 2010 — five days before the BP explosion on April 20 [S3]. The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote; it died in referral [S1, S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who today can be left covering cleanup costs beyond a spill's $75 million liability cap; coastal residents, fishermen, and tourism businesses that suffer spill damages and would no longer face a cap on what they can recover; and by extension anyone exposed to a future offshore spill, since unlimited liability gives companies a stronger financial reason to avoid one.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law an offshore spiller owes all removal costs plus damages only up to $75 million; the bill strikes the cap so the responsible party pays everything [S2, S3].

The change takes effect April 15, 2010, which would cover the BP Deepwater Horizon spill that began days later, meaning the company causing the largest spill in U.S. history could not hide behind the cap [S3].
The bill was introduced with 24 Senate cosponsors in its first week, all from the Democratic caucus plus the chamber's Independent [S4, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies that drill offshore would bear the full cost of their own spills, and their insurers and investors would carry the risk. Industry groups argued that unlimited liability could push smaller and mid-sized drillers (and their insurance markets) out of deepwater work, which supporters of the cap said would slow domestic offshore production.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability can be unpredictable: the bill sets no ceiling at all, so even small operators could face ruinous exposure from a single incident, and critics warned this could concentrate offshore drilling in the hands of the largest companies or raise insurance costs.
The retroactive effective date raises a fair-process objection: it changes the legal rules for a spill that had already occurred, penalizing conduct done under the old $75 million cap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a straightforward shift of spill costs from taxpayers and victims onto the companies that profit from drilling, which is why it drew two dozen Democratic cosponsors within days of the BP disaster. The honest objections are that a hard zero cap creates uncertainty that could squeeze out smaller operators and raise drilling insurance costs, and that making the rule retroactive to cover the BP spill is aggressive. A graduated or high cap would have answered the first concern; the bill chose simplicity instead.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 9, 2010, read twice, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5, S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 9, 2010 by Senator Menendez with 24 cosponsors, two months after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion began the largest offshore oil spill in U.S. history [S3, S4].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, which was the bill's last official action [S5].
Congress.gov records no further committee or floor action for the remainder of the 111th Congress, which ended January 3, 2011 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies came out ahead: the $75 million liability cap stayed in place, so they and their insurers kept the ceiling on what they must pay for any future spill, and taxpayers and coastal victims kept the residual risk. The EPW Committee's decision not to act was the mechanism that preserved the status quo [S5, S2].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies kept the liability cap

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 3472 on June 9, 2010, to remove the $75 million offshore spill liability cap [S3].

for.name: 23 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill within days of introduction [S4].

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the chamber's only Independent [S4].

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or report — from referral on June 9, 2010 through the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: American Petroleum Institute
against.role: Offshore oil and gas industry trade association
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against removing the liability cap, warning that unlimited liability would harm offshore drilling economics; the effort was widely reported during the 2010 spill-response fight in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors came from the Democratic caucus or its Independent; no Senate Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-held minority plus the committee's inaction left the bill nowhere [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose was to remove the $75 million cap on their spill liability, making them pay all cleanup and damage costs. Its death left the cap intact, which is why the industry's position ran against the interests of taxpayers and coastal residents [S2, S3].
Unlimited liability would raise the risk they underwrite for offshore drilling; that cost could flow back into drilling economics and insurance premiums [S3].

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses bear the economic damage of spills and would no longer face a cap on what a spiller owes them, since the bill makes the responsible party liable for all damages [S2].
